name: Alarcos
summary: A hilltop fortress on the Guadiana near Ciudad Real, still unfinished when Alfonso VIII of Castile was destroyed beneath its walls by the Almohads on 18 July 1195.
overview: Alarcos guarded the exposed southern frontier of Castile toward al-Andalus. Its name belongs to the worst Castilian defeat of the twelfth century, fought below its half-built walls in 1195.
knownFor: An unfinished frontier castle that could not shelter a beaten army
The Almohad recovery of the Castilian frontier
An archaeological park over an Iberian oppidum and a medieval castle

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Alarcos occupies a low hill above the river Guadiana a few kilometres west of modern Ciudad Real. In the twelfth century this was the outer edge of Castilian settlement, the last defensible ground before the empty country of the Campo de Calatrava and the passes leading south to Almohad Andalusia.

Alfonso VIII of Castile was fortifying the hill as a frontier stronghold and planned town when the Almohad caliph moved north. The castle was not finished, and the battle fought beneath it on 18 July 1195 wrecked Castilian power on the frontier for a generation.

contentSections.title: The battle of 1195
paragraphs: Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur crossed from Morocco with a large army and advanced on the half-built fortress. Alfonso VIII chose to give battle at once rather than wait for the contingents of León and Navarre, which were still on the road — a decision usually explained by an underestimate of Almohad numbers, or by a fear that waiting would let the caliph into the Tagus valley behind him.

The Castilian heavy cavalry charged first and broke the Almohad front, scattering the Zenata and Banu Marin horse and killing the vizier Abu Yahya. The reserve then closed on both flanks while al-Mansur's own division came up, and the Castilians were surrounded. Alfonso escaped toward Toledo; the bishops of Ávila, Segovia and Sigüenza were killed, along with much of the nobility and the commanders of the military orders, and Diego López de Haro shut the survivors in the unfinished castle, which surrendered.

contentSections.title: What the defeat cost
paragraphs: The Almohads took Alarcos and followed the victory by recovering Calatrava, Malagón, Benavente and, in the campaigns of the next two years, Trujillo, Montánchez, Plasencia and Talavera. The frontier was pushed back toward the Tagus, and Castile spent years in a defensive crouch complicated by war with León and Navarre.

The reversal came seventeen years later. The coalition Alfonso assembled with Aragon and Navarre and a papal crusading bull broke the Almohad field army at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, and Alarcos itself was recovered soon after. Alfonso died in 1214, at the village of Gutierre-Muñoz in Ávila province.

contentSections.title: The site
paragraphs: The hill has been excavated since the 1980s and is now an archaeological park. Beneath and around the medieval remains lies a substantial Iberian oppidum, occupied from the Bronze Age and heavily built in the Iron Age, so the Castilian castle was reusing a site already old when it was chosen.

The medieval remains include the castle enceinte with its towers, streets and houses of the planned town that was never completed, and the church of Santa María de Alarcos, a thirteenth-century building on the summit that later became a sanctuary and is still a place of local pilgrimage.

contentSections.title: Alarcos and Ciudad Real
paragraphs: The settlement never recovered its intended role. When Alfonso X founded Villa Real — the future Ciudad Real — a short distance away in 1255, the new town drew off whatever population and function Alarcos retained, and the hill was left to the church and the fields.

That abandonment is why the site is archaeologically valuable: an aborted twelfth-century frontier town, sealed by desertion rather than buried under a living city, with the battlefield that ended it lying open below.

timeline.title: The fortress begun
timeline.description: Alfonso VIII starts building a castle and planned town on the hill to anchor the southern frontier.

timeline.title: Battle of Alarcos
timeline.description: Alfonso VIII attacks without waiting for his allies and is enveloped by the army of Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur.

timeline.title: The castle surrenders
timeline.description: Diego López de Haro holds the unfinished walls with the survivors and gives them up to the Almohads.

timeline.title: The frontier falls back
timeline.description: Almohad campaigns take Calatrava, Trujillo, Montánchez and Talavera, pressing Castile toward the Tagus.

timeline.title: Las Navas de Tolosa
timeline.description: The Iberian coalition breaks the Almohad field army, reversing the verdict of Alarcos.

timeline.title: Villa Real founded
timeline.description: Alfonso X's new town nearby, later Ciudad Real, ends any prospect of Alarcos being rebuilt.

imageInfo.caption: The hill and battlefield of Alarcos above the Guadiana near Ciudad Real, in a 2009 photograph.
imageInfo.creator: Valdavia (Wikimedia Commons)
imageInfo.note: A wide panorama of the ground rather than a view of a monument, which suits the subject: the open plain below the ridge is where the Castilian army was enveloped in 1195, and the sanctuary and excavated castle on the skyline mark the fortress Alfonso VIII was still building when the Almohads arrived.
